Lecture 1 · M2 Digital Modulation · CO2

Why send bits instead of waveforms?

An analog repeater amplifies the noise along with the signal, so a 20-hop link ends up 13 dB worse than one hop. A digital repeater decides what each bit was and sends a clean copy. That single idea is why every modern system is digital.

Explain regeneration and noise accumulationCompute bit rate, baud and bandwidthState Shannon capacityList the advantages and costs of digital
⏱ 50 minBTL-2 Understand · BTL-3 Apply

ConceptFour reasons the world went digital

Regeneration

A repeater only has to decide "0 or 1". If it decides correctly the noise is gone completely; analog repeaters can never remove noise.

Robustness and coding

Error-control codes (Module 5) detect and correct errors. Analog signals have no equivalent.

Multiplexing and integration

Voice, video and data are all just bits: one network carries everything, time- or frequency-shared (Module 4).

Processing and security

Bits can be compressed, encrypted, stored and processed by cheap digital hardware and software radios.

Analogy: photocopy of a photocopyCopy a photograph 20 times on an analog copier and it becomes grey mush. Copy a text file 20 times and it is perfect, because each copy re-reads the letters. A digital repeater is the text-file copier.
Cost of going digitalHow it is handled
More bandwidth than the analog message (64 kb/s for 4 kHz voice)Compression, higher-order modulation (L3, L4)
Needs synchronisation (carrier, symbol timing)PLL, Costas loop, timing recovery (M3)
Quantisation noiseEnough bits per sample (SGPS course)
Threshold effect: works perfectly, then fails abruptlyLink margin, adaptive modulation (L7)

DerivationNoise accumulation, bit rate, baud and capacity

A · Analog chain versus digital chain

  1. Each of \(N\) identical analog hops adds noise power \(N_h\) while the signal is restored to \(S\). The noise powers add:

    \[ \text{SNR}_N=\frac{S}{N\,N_h}=\frac{\text{SNR}_1}{N}\quad\Rightarrow\quad \text{SNR}_N(\text{dB})=\text{SNR}_1(\text{dB})-10\log_{10}N \]

  2. Each digital hop makes an independent bit error with probability \(p\). An end-to-end error happens if an odd number of hops err; for small \(p\):

    \[ P_{e,N}=1-(1-p)^N\approx Np \]

    Compare: with BPSK at 10 dB per hop, \(p=3.9\times10^{-6}\); 20 hops give \(7.7\times10^{-5}\), still excellent. The analog chain has lost 13 dB.

B · Bit rate, symbol rate and bandwidth

  1. A modulation with \(M\) symbols carries \(k=\log_2M\) bits per symbol. Bit rate \(R_b\) and symbol (baud) rate \(R_s\) are related by

    \[ R_s=\frac{R_b}{\log_2 M}\ \text{baud},\qquad T_s=kT_b \]

  2. With Nyquist pulses of roll-off \(\alpha\) (Module 3), the passband bandwidth is \(B=R_s(1+\alpha)\), so the spectral efficiency is

    \[ \eta=\frac{R_b}{B}=\frac{\log_2M}{1+\alpha}\ \text{bit/s/Hz} \]

  3. Shannon capacity sets the absolute limit for any modulation and coding on an AWGN channel of bandwidth \(B\):

    \[ C=B\log_2\!\left(1+\frac{S}{N}\right)\ \text{bit/s} \]

    Meaning: no scheme can send error-free faster than \(C\); every lecture in this module measures how close a practical scheme gets.

C · Energy per bit

  1. Received power \(P_r\) spread over \(R_b\) bits per second gives energy per bit \(E_b=P_r/R_b\). With noise PSD \(N_0\):

    \[ \frac{E_b}{N_0}=\frac{P_r}{N_0R_b}=\text{SNR}\cdot\frac{B}{R_b} \]

    Why this measure: \(E_b/N_0\) lets us compare schemes with different bit rates and bandwidths fairly; all BER curves use it.

InteractiveAnalog repeaters versus regenerative repeaters

Top: output SNR versus hops. For the digital chain the "equivalent SNR" is shown as 10 log(1/4Pe), capped at 40 dB. Bottom: the same bit pattern after N hops.

Worked examplesSolved numericals

Example 1 · Telephone PCM bit rate
Given: voice sampled at 8 kHz, 8 bits per sample.

\(R_b=8000\times8=64\) kb/s. One analog voice channel (4 kHz) becomes a 64 kb/s stream: the bandwidth cost of digital.

Answer: 64 kb/s (the DS0 channel).

Example 2 · Analog vs digital chain regeneration
Given: 10 hops, 30 dB SNR per hop (analog); BPSK at \(E_b/N_0=10\) dB per hop (digital).

Analog: \(30-10\log 10=20\) dB. Digital: \(p=Q(\sqrt{20})=3.87\times10^{-6}\), \(P_e\approx10p=3.9\times10^{-5}\).

Answer: 20 dB SNR (analog) vs BER 3.9 × 10⁻⁵ (digital).

Example 3 · Baud symbol rate
Given: 9600 b/s modem using 16-QAM.

\(k=4\), \(R_s=9600/4=2400\) baud.

Answer: 2400 baud.

Example 4 · Shannon limit of a phone line capacity
Given: \(B=3.1\) kHz, SNR = 30 dB.

\(C=3100\log_2(1001)=3100\times9.967=30.9\) kb/s. V.34 modems reached 33.6 kb/s using a slightly wider band and better SNR.

Answer: about 30.9 kb/s.

Example 5 · Bandwidth of a QPSK signal spectral efficiency
Given: \(R_b=2\) Mb/s QPSK, roll-off 0.25.

\(R_s=1\) Mbaud, \(B=R_s(1+\alpha)=1.25\) MHz, \(\eta=2/1.25=1.6\) bit/s/Hz.

Answer: 1.25 MHz, 1.6 bit/s/Hz.

Real worldWhere you meet this

Optical fibre

Regenerators every 80–100 km made trans-oceanic digital links possible; analog cables could not match them.

Digital TV switch-over

One 8 MHz analog TV channel now carries 4–6 digital programmes (DVB-T2, ATSC 3.0).

Your phone call

Voice is coded at 8–24 kb/s (AMR, EVS), sent as bits over 4G/5G, and regenerated at every hop of the core network.

Common mistakesWatch out

  • Confusing bit rate and baud: they are equal only for binary modulation.
  • Comparing schemes by SNR instead of Eb/N0 when their bit rates differ.
  • Thinking digital has no noise: it has noise, but decisions remove it until the threshold is crossed.

Lecture 2 · M2 Digital Modulation · CO2

BPSK: two points, one threshold, one famous formula

Flip the carrier phase by 180° for a 1 and you have the most noise-robust binary modulation there is. Its error rate, \(Q(\sqrt{2E_b/N_0})\), is the yardstick every other scheme is measured against.

Write the BPSK signal and its signal-space formDerive the correlator output and the BERFind BPSK bandwidth and PSDCompare coherent BPSK with DPSK
⏱ 50 minBTL-3 Apply

ConceptThe signal and its picture

For each bit of duration \(T_b\):

\[ s_i(t)=\pm\sqrt{\frac{2E_b}{T_b}}\cos(2\pi f_ct),\quad 0\le t\lt T_b \]

Signal space

One unit-energy basis function \(\phi(t)=\sqrt{2/T_b}\cos(2\pi f_ct)\). The two signals are points \(\pm\sqrt{E_b}\) on a line: distance \(d=2\sqrt{E_b}\).

Antipodal

The two points are opposite each other. For a given energy, antipodal signals have the largest possible distance, which is why BPSK is optimal among binary schemes.

Analogy: a coin on a lineNoise nudges a coin placed at +1 or −1. You call "1" if it ends up right of zero. Errors happen only when noise pushes it all the way past the middle: a distance of √Eb.

DerivationCorrelator receiver and the error probability

  1. Received signal: \(r(t)=s_i(t)+w(t)\), with \(w(t)\) white Gaussian noise of two-sided PSD \(N_0/2\).

  2. Correlate with the basis function over one bit:

    \[ z=\int_0^{T_b}r(t)\phi(t)\,dt=\pm\sqrt{E_b}+n,\qquad n=\int_0^{T_b}w(t)\phi(t)\,dt \]

  3. Noise statistics: \(n\) is Gaussian with mean 0 and variance

    \[ \sigma^2=E\!\left[\iint w(t)w(\tau)\phi(t)\phi(\tau)\,dt\,d\tau\right]=\frac{N_0}{2}\int_0^{T_b}\phi^2(t)\,dt=\frac{N_0}{2} \]

    Step: \(E[w(t)w(\tau)]=\tfrac{N_0}{2}\delta(t-\tau)\) and \(\phi\) has unit energy.

  4. Decide "1" if \(z>0\). By symmetry the error probability is the chance that the noise exceeds \(\sqrt{E_b}\):

    \[ P_b=P(n>\sqrt{E_b})=Q\!\left(\frac{\sqrt{E_b}}{\sigma}\right) \]

  5. Substitute \(\sigma=\sqrt{N_0/2}\):

    \[ P_b=Q\!\left(\sqrt{\frac{2E_b}{N_0}}\right),\qquad Q(x)=\frac1{\sqrt{2\pi}}\int_x^\infty e^{-u^2/2}du=\tfrac12\operatorname{erfc}\!\left(\frac{x}{\sqrt2}\right) \]

    General form: the argument is \(d/(2\sigma)\) with \(d=2\sqrt{E_b}\): only the distance between points and the noise level matter.

Spectrum and bandwidth

  1. BPSK is a random ±1 rectangular pulse train times a carrier. The baseband PSD of random NRZ pulses is \(E_b\,\text{sinc}^2(fT_b)\), shifted to \(\pm f_c\):

    \[ S(f)=\frac{E_b}{2}\left[\text{sinc}^2\big((f-f_c)T_b\big)+\text{sinc}^2\big((f+f_c)T_b\big)\right] \]

  2. Nulls at \(f_c\pm R_b\): null-to-null bandwidth \(B=2R_b\). With raised-cosine pulses (M3) this falls to \(R_b(1+\alpha)\).

Non-coherent cousin: DPSK

Differential PSK encodes each bit as a phase change and detects it by comparing consecutive symbols, so no carrier recovery is needed. The price is about 1 dB at BER \(10^{-5}\):

\[ P_{b,\text{DPSK}}=\tfrac12e^{-E_b/N_0} \]

InteractiveInside the correlator

Top: BPSK waveform for 8 bits, clean (blue) and noisy (grey). Bottom: Gaussian pdfs of the correlator output for each bit; the shaded tails past the threshold are the error probability.

Worked examplesSolved numericals

Example 1 · BER from link values Q-function
Given: \(R_b=1\) Mb/s, received amplitude 2 mV across 1 Ω, \(N_0=10^{-13}\) W/Hz.

\(E_b=A^2T_b/2=(4\times10^{-6})(10^{-6})/2=2\times10^{-12}\) J. \(E_b/N_0=20\) (13 dB). \(P_b=Q(\sqrt{40})=Q(6.32)\).

Answer: 1.27 × 10⁻¹⁰.

Example 2 · Eb/N0 for a target BER inverse Q
Given: \(P_b=10^{-6}\).

\(Q(x)=10^{-6}\Rightarrow x=4.753\). \(2E_b/N_0=22.59\Rightarrow E_b/N_0=11.30\).

Answer: 10.5 dB.

Example 3 · Bandwidth spectrum
Given: \(R_b=10\) kb/s rectangular BPSK.

Null-to-null \(2R_b=20\) kHz centred on \(f_c\).

Answer: 20 kHz.

Example 4 · BPSK vs DPSK non-coherent
Given: \(E_b/N_0=10\) dB.

BPSK \(Q(\sqrt{20})=3.87\times10^{-6}\). DPSK \(\tfrac12e^{-10}=2.27\times10^{-5}\).

Answer: DPSK is about 6× worse at this Eb/N0 (≈ 1 dB penalty).

Example 5 · Carrier phase error imperfect sync
Given: \(E_b/N_0=10\) dB, receiver phase error 25°.

The correlator output shrinks by \(\cos25^\circ=0.906\), so the effective \(E_b\) drops by \(\cos^2\): \(P_b=Q(\sqrt{20\times0.821})=Q(4.05)\).

Answer: 2.5 × 10⁻⁵ (6.5× worse than perfect sync).

Real worldWhere you meet this

Deep-space probes

Voyager and many CubeSats use BPSK (with powerful codes) because every fraction of a dB matters at billions of kilometres.

GPS

Each satellite sends BPSK-modulated spreading codes at 1575.42 MHz, received far below the noise floor.

5G NR uplink

π/2-BPSK is used with DFT-s-OFDM for cell-edge phones: low peak power, long battery life.

Common mistakesWatch out

  • Writing \(Q(\sqrt{E_b/N_0})\) for BPSK. That is coherent BFSK (orthogonal), 3 dB worse.
  • Forgetting to convert dB to linear before taking the square root.
  • Using an envelope detector for BPSK: the envelope is constant, all information is in the phase.

Lecture 3 · M2 Digital Modulation · CO2

QPSK doubles the bits for free; 8-PSK makes you pay

Put one BPSK on the cosine and another on the sine and you send two bits per symbol in the same bandwidth with the same BER. Squeeze in more phases and each extra bit costs you about 4–6 dB.

Build QPSK from two BPSK streamsDerive the M-PSK symbol error rateCompute bandwidth efficiencyExplain OQPSK and π/4-QPSK
⏱ 50 minBTL-3 Apply

ConceptIn-phase and quadrature

Two carriers \(\cos\omega_ct\) and \(-\sin\omega_ct\) are orthogonal over a symbol. Any passband signal can be written with an I and a Q part:

\[ s(t)=I(t)\cos\omega_ct-Q(t)\sin\omega_ct=\Re\{[I(t)+jQ(t)]e^{j\omega_ct}\} \]

QPSK

\(I,Q\in\{\pm1\}/\sqrt2\): four points at 45°, 135°, 225°, 315°. Two bits per symbol, Gray-labelled so neighbours differ in one bit.

M-PSK

\(M\) points equally spaced on a circle: \(s_k=\sqrt{E_s}e^{j2\pi k/M}\). Constant envelope, so it suits saturated amplifiers (satellites).

Analogy: two independent lanesI and Q are two lanes of a road that never touch. QPSK puts one BPSK car in each lane: twice the traffic, each car just as safe.

DerivationQPSK BER and the M-PSK symbol error rate

A · QPSK is two BPSKs

  1. With Gray mapping, bit 1 rides on I and bit 2 on Q. Each axis is BPSK with energy \(E_s/2=E_b\) per bit, and the I and Q noises are independent with variance \(N_0/2\).

  2. Each bit therefore sees the BPSK error rate:

    \[ P_{b,\text{QPSK}}=Q\!\left(\sqrt{\frac{2E_b}{N_0}}\right) \]

  3. A symbol is correct only if both bits are:

    \[ P_{s}=1-\left[1-Q\!\left(\sqrt{E_s/N_0}\right)\right]^2=2Q(\sqrt{E_s/N_0})-Q^2(\sqrt{E_s/N_0}) \]

    Result: same BER as BPSK, half the bandwidth per bit. QPSK is the workhorse of satellite TV, 4G/5G control channels and Wi-Fi at the cell edge.

B · M-PSK

  1. Adjacent points on a circle of radius \(\sqrt{E_s}\) are separated by angle \(2\pi/M\). Their distance is the chord:

    \[ d_{\min}=2\sqrt{E_s}\sin\frac{\pi}{M} \]

  2. An error occurs mainly when noise pushes the point past one of its two neighbouring decision boundaries, each at distance \(d_{\min}/2\):

    \[ P_s\approx2Q\!\left(\frac{d_{\min}/2}{\sqrt{N_0/2}}\right) \]

  3. Substitute \(d_{\min}\) and \(E_s=E_b\log_2M\):

    \[ P_s\approx2Q\!\left(\sqrt{\frac{2E_s}{N_0}}\sin\frac{\pi}{M}\right),\qquad P_b\approx\frac{P_s}{\log_2M}\ (\text{Gray}) \]

    Cost: doubling M halves \(\sin(\pi/M)\) for large M: 6 dB more \(E_s/N_0\), or about 4–5 dB more \(E_b/N_0\) once the extra bit is counted.

C · Bandwidth efficiency and variants

  1. All M-PSK schemes occupy \(B=R_s(1+\alpha)\); bits per hertz rise as \(\log_2M\): BPSK 1, QPSK 2, 8-PSK 3 bit/s/Hz with ideal Nyquist pulses.

  2. OQPSK delays Q by half a symbol so I and Q never switch together: no 180° jumps, smaller envelope dips after filtering. π/4-QPSK alternates between two QPSK sets rotated by 45°, so maximum phase step is 135° (used in TETRA, older US cellular).

InteractiveDecision wedges of M-PSK

Dashed lines are the decision boundaries. Each wedge is 360°/M wide; a symbol error happens when a point lands in the wrong wedge.

Worked examplesSolved numericals

Example 1 · QPSK bandwidth efficiency
Given: \(R_b=2\) Mb/s, rectangular pulses.

\(R_s=1\) Mbaud; null-to-null \(2R_s=2\) MHz (BPSK needs 4 MHz).

Answer: 2 MHz.

Example 2 · 8-PSK symbol error rate M-PSK
Given: \(E_s/N_0=16\) dB (39.8).

\(\sqrt{2\times39.8}\sin22.5^\circ=8.92\times0.383=3.41\); \(P_s\approx2Q(3.41)\).

Answer: 6.4 × 10⁻⁴.

Example 3 · Cost of 8-PSK over QPSK penalty
Given: same symbol error rate, Gray coding.

Equal Q arguments: QPSK \(2E_s\sin^2(\pi/4)=2E_b\); 8-PSK \(2(3E_b)\sin^2(\pi/8)=0.879E_b\). Ratio \(2/0.879=2.28\).

Answer: 3.6 dB more Eb/N0.

Example 4 · Cost of 16-PSK over 8-PSK penalty
Given: same symbol error rate.

\(\dfrac{3\sin^2(\pi/8)}{4\sin^2(\pi/16)}=\dfrac{0.439}{0.152}=2.89\).

Answer: 4.6 dB more Eb/N0.

Example 5 · QPSK symbol error rate exact
Given: \(E_s/N_0=10\) dB.

\(q=Q(\sqrt{10})=7.83\times10^{-4}\); \(P_s=2q-q^2\).

Answer: 1.56 × 10⁻³.

DVB-S2 satellite TV

Common mistakesWatch out

  • Thinking QPSK has a worse BER than BPSK. Per bit, with Gray coding, they are identical.
  • Using \(E_b\) instead of \(E_s\) in the M-PSK formula.
  • Forgetting that the M-PSK formula is an approximation, poor at low SNR for M = 4.

Lecture 4 · M2 Digital Modulation · CO2

QAM: fill the plane with points, not just a circle

For 16 points, spreading them on a 4 × 4 grid gives 4.2 dB more distance than squeezing them on a circle. That is why Wi-Fi, 4G, 5G, cable modems and DSL all use QAM.

Construct square M-QAM constellationsDerive average energy and dminCompute the QAM symbol error rateRead impairments and EVM from a constellation
⏱ 50 minBTL-3 Apply · BTL-4 Analyse

ConceptTwo PAM signals in quadrature

Square M-QAM sends an \(m\)-level PAM on I and another on Q, with \(m=\sqrt M\). Levels are \(\{\pm d,\pm3d,\dots,\pm(m-1)d\}\).

SchemeGridbits/symbolEs (d = 1)dmin/√EsPeak/average
QPSK = 4-QAM2 × 2221.4141.00 (0 dB)
16-QAM4 × 44100.6321.80 (2.55 dB)
64-QAM8 × 86420.3092.33 (3.68 dB)
256-QAM16 × 1681700.1532.65 (4.23 dB)
1024-QAM32 × 32106820.0772.82 (4.50 dB)

Why not PSK?

For M = 16, PSK puts all points on one circle; QAM uses the whole plane, so points are further apart for the same average power.

The price

QAM has a varying envelope (peak ≠ average), so the power amplifier must be linear and backed off. Amplitude and phase errors both matter.

DerivationAverage energy, minimum distance and error rate

  1. One PAM axis. The \(m\) levels \((2i-m-1)d\) have mean square

    \[ \frac1m\sum_{i=1}^{m}(2i-m-1)^2d^2=\frac{(m^2-1)d^2}{3} \]

    Step: sum of the squares of the odd numbers \(1,3,\dots,m-1\) taken on both sides of zero.

  2. Both axes:

    \[ E_s=2\cdot\frac{(m^2-1)d^2}{3}=\frac{2(M-1)}{3}d^2 \]

    Points are \(2d\) apart, so

    \[ d_{\min}=2d=\sqrt{\frac{6E_s}{M-1}} \]

  3. Error on one axis. Inner levels can err to either side, the two outer ones to one side only. Averaging over levels:

    \[ P_{\text{PAM}}=2\left(1-\frac1{\sqrt M}\right)Q\!\left(\frac{d}{\sqrt{N_0/2}}\right)=2\left(1-\frac1{\sqrt M}\right)Q\!\left(\sqrt{\frac{3E_s}{(M-1)N_0}}\right) \]

  4. Symbol error if either axis errs:

    \[ P_s=1-(1-P_{\text{PAM}})^2\approx4\left(1-\frac1{\sqrt M}\right)Q\!\left(\sqrt{\frac{3E_s}{(M-1)N_0}}\right),\quad P_b\approx\frac{P_s}{\log_2M} \]

    Rule of thumb: each 4× increase in M (two more bits) needs about 6 dB more \(E_s/N_0\): \(M-1\) roughly quadruples.

Error vector magnitude

  1. Transmitters and receivers are tested by the error vector between each received point and its ideal position:

    \[ \text{EVM}_{\text{rms}}=\sqrt{\frac{\frac1N\sum|r_k-s_k|^2}{\frac1N\sum|s_k|^2}},\qquad \text{SNR}\approx-20\log_{10}\text{EVM} \]

    Use: with only AWGN, EVM² is the noise-to-signal ratio. Phase noise, I/Q imbalance, carrier offset and amplifier compression all add to it, and each leaves a recognisable shape on the constellation.

InteractiveImpairments on a QAM constellation

Phase offset rotates the whole constellation (outer points move most). Gain imbalance stretches I relative to Q. Dashed lines are the decision boundaries.

Worked examplesSolved numericals

Example 1 · 16-QAM energy and PAPR constellation
Given: 16-QAM with levels ±1, ±3.

\(E_s=2(16-1)/3=10\). Corner points have energy \(3^2+3^2=18\). Peak/average \(=1.8\).

Answer: Es = 10, PAPR = 2.55 dB.

Example 2 · 16-QAM versus 16-PSK distance
Given: equal average energy \(E_s=1\).

QAM: \(\sqrt{6/15}=0.632\). PSK: \(2\sin(\pi/16)=0.390\). Ratio in dB: \(20\log(0.632/0.390)\).

Answer: QAM has 4.2 dB more distance.

Example 3 · 64-QAM symbol error rate formula
Given: \(E_s/N_0=25\) dB (316).

\(\sqrt{3\times316/63}=3.88\). \(P_s\approx4(1-\tfrac18)Q(3.88)=3.5\times5.2\times10^{-5}\).

Answer: 1.8 × 10⁻⁴; BER ≈ 3 × 10⁻⁵.

Example 4 · EVM to SNR measurement
Given: measured EVM = 3 %.

\(\text{SNR}\approx-20\log_{10}0.03=30.5\) dB: enough for 256-QAM (limit 3.5 %).

Answer: ≈ 30.5 dB.

Example 5 · Data rate capacity of a channel
Given: 256-QAM, 20 MHz channel, roll-off 0.25.

\(R_s=20/1.25=16\) Mbaud; \(R_b=8\times16=128\) Mb/s (before coding).

Answer: 128 Mb/s.

Common mistakesWatch out

  • Using the peak energy instead of the average energy in error formulas.
  • Forgetting that BER ≈ SER/log₂M only holds with Gray mapping and at moderate-to-high SNR.
  • Running a QAM signal through a saturated amplifier: the outer points get squashed (AM/AM compression).

Lecture 5 · M2 Digital Modulation · CO2

BER analysis: from a link budget to a number of errors per second

Every BER formula is the same idea: distance between points divided by the noise spread, pushed through the Q-function. Learn to move between Eb/N0, SNR and received power, and you can predict any link before building it.

Use the Q-function and its boundsConvert between SNR, Eb/N0 and received powerCompare schemes on a BER chartPlan a Monte-Carlo BER measurement
⏱ 50 minBTL-3 Apply · BTL-4 Analyse

ConceptThe AWGN channel and the Q-function

AWGN model

\(r(t)=s(t)+w(t)\), with \(w\) Gaussian, zero mean, flat PSD \(N_0/2\). It models thermal noise and is the baseline for every receiver test.

Q-function

\(Q(x)=P(Z>x)\) for a standard normal \(Z\). It falls very fast: \(Q(3)=1.35\times10^{-3}\), \(Q(4)=3.2\times10^{-5}\), \(Q(5)=2.9\times10^{-7}\).

Scheme (coherent, AWGN, Gray)Bit error rateEb/N0 for 10⁻⁵
BPSK, QPSK\(Q(\sqrt{2E_b/N_0})\)9.6 dB
DPSK\(\tfrac12e^{-E_b/N_0}\)10.3 dB
Coherent BFSK (orthogonal)\(Q(\sqrt{E_b/N_0})\)12.6 dB
8-PSK\(\tfrac23Q(\sqrt{6E_b/N_0}\sin\frac\pi8)\)13.0 dB
16-QAM\(\tfrac34Q(\sqrt{\tfrac45E_b/N_0})\)13.4 dB
64-QAM\(\tfrac7{12}Q(\sqrt{\tfrac27E_b/N_0})\)17.8 dB

Required Eb/N0 values from the formulas in the table (nearest-neighbour approximations), computed numerically.

DerivationFrom distance to BER, and from watts to Eb/N0

A · The general binary detector

  1. Two signals separated by Euclidean distance \(d\). Project onto the line joining them: the noise along that line has variance \(N_0/2\); the threshold is halfway.

    \[ P_b=Q\!\left(\frac{d}{2\sigma}\right)=Q\!\left(\sqrt{\frac{d^2}{2N_0}}\right) \]

  2. Antipodal (BPSK): \(d^2=4E_b\Rightarrow Q(\sqrt{2E_b/N_0})\). Orthogonal (BFSK): \(d^2=2E_b\Rightarrow Q(\sqrt{E_b/N_0})\), a 3 dB loss.

  3. Union bound for M signals:

    \[ P_s\le\sum_{j\ne i}Q\!\left(\frac{d_{ij}}{2\sigma}\right)\approx N_{\min}Q\!\left(\frac{d_{\min}}{2\sigma}\right) \]

    with \(N_{\min}\) the number of nearest neighbours. This is where the "2" in M-PSK and the "4(1−1/√M)" in QAM come from.

  4. Chernoff bound \(Q(x)\le\tfrac12e^{-x^2/2}\): handy for quick estimates and for seeing that BER falls exponentially in \(E_b/N_0\).

B · Link budget to Eb/N0

  1. Thermal noise PSD at room temperature: \(N_0=kT\approx-174\) dBm/Hz, plus the receiver noise figure NF.

  2. In decibels:

    \[ \frac{E_b}{N_0}\Big|_{\text{dB}}=P_r|_{\text{dBm}}-\big(-174+\text{NF}\big)-10\log_{10}R_b \]

  3. Then BER from the chart, and the packet error rate for an \(L\)-bit packet: \(\text{PER}=1-(1-P_b)^L\approx LP_b\).

C · Measuring BER by simulation

  1. Count errors \(N_e\) in \(N\) bits: \(\hat P_b=N_e/N\). The count is roughly Poisson, so its relative standard deviation is \(1/\sqrt{N_e}\). Rule: simulate until you see at least 100 errors (±10 %). For \(P_b=10^{-6}\) that is \(10^8\) bits.

InteractiveBER chart explorer

Curves are the nearest-neighbour formulas (BER ≈ SER/log₂M with Gray mapping). The readout gives each scheme’s BER at the marker and the Eb/N0 it needs for the target.

Worked examplesSolved numericals

Example 1 · SNR to Eb/N0 conversion
Given: \(R_b=1\) Mb/s, noise bandwidth \(B=1.25\) MHz, SNR = 10 dB.

\(E_b/N_0=\text{SNR}+10\log(B/R_b)=10+0.97\).

Answer: 10.97 dB.

Example 2 · BPSK versus coherent BFSK antipodal vs orthogonal
Given: \(E_b/N_0=10\) dB.

BPSK \(Q(\sqrt{20})=3.87\times10^{-6}\); BFSK \(Q(\sqrt{10})=7.83\times10^{-4}\).

Answer: BFSK is 200× worse (3 dB).

Example 3 · Chernoff estimate bound
Given: BPSK at 10 dB.

\(\tfrac12e^{-10}=2.27\times10^{-5}\) versus exact \(3.87\times10^{-6}\).

Answer: Bound is 6× too high, but quick.

Example 4 · Link budget received power
Given: \(P_r=-100\) dBm, NF = 0 dB, \(R_b=1\) Mb/s, BPSK.

\(E_b/N_0=-100+174-60=14\) dB (25.1). \(P_b=Q(\sqrt{50.2})=Q(7.09)\).

Answer: ≈ 7 × 10⁻¹³: essentially error-free.

Example 5 · Packet error rate PER
Given: 1000-bit packets, \(P_b=10^{-5}\).

\(\text{PER}=1-(1-10^{-5})^{1000}\approx0.00995\).

Answer: about 1 % of packets lost.

Lecture 6 · M2 Digital Modulation · CO2

Symbol errors become bit errors: Gray coding keeps it to one

Noise almost always pushes a point to its nearest neighbour. Label neighbours so they differ in just one bit, and each symbol error costs one bit instead of up to log₂M. That labelling is the Gray code.

Relate SER and BERConstruct and decode Gray codesGray-label PSK and QAM constellationsQuantify the penalty of natural binary
⏱ 40 minBTL-3 Apply

ConceptSER is not BER

A detector chooses symbols. If a symbol error flips \(h\) of the \(k=\log_2M\) bits, the bit error rate is \(P_b=\bar h\,P_s/k\), where \(\bar h\) is the average number of bits that differ between the sent symbol and the one chosen.

CaseBER in terms of SER
Best case (Gray, high SNR)\(P_b\approx P_s/k\)
Worst case\(P_b\le P_s\)
M orthogonal signals (FSK)\(P_b=\frac{M/2}{M-1}P_s\)
Analogy: house numbersIf neighbouring houses had numbers 0111 and 1000, a postman one door off would get all four digits wrong. Gray numbering makes neighbours differ in one digit only.

DerivationGray codes: build, convert, apply

  1. Reflect-and-prefix: start with 0, 1. Reflect the list and prefix the original half with 0 and the reflected half with 1: 00, 01, 11, 10. Repeat: 000, 001, 011, 010, 110, 111, 101, 100.

  2. Binary to Gray (bitwise XOR with a one-bit shift):

    \[ g=b\oplus(b\gg1),\qquad g_{k-1}=b_{k-1},\ g_i=b_{i+1}\oplus b_i \]

  3. Gray to binary (running XOR from the top bit): \(b_{k-1}=g_{k-1},\ b_i=b_{i+1}\oplus g_i\).

  4. M-PSK: assign Gray codes to points in order around the circle; the last and first codes also differ in one bit, so the wrap-around neighbour is fine.

  5. Square QAM: Gray-code the I index and the Q index separately and concatenate: \(\ell=(g_I\ll k/2)\,|\,g_Q\). Horizontal neighbours differ only in the I part, vertical ones only in Q.

  6. Natural binary penalty. For 8-PSK with labels 0…7 in order, the eight neighbour pairs differ in 1, 2, 1, 3, 1, 2, 1, 3 bits: \(\bar h=14/8=1.75\). The BER is 75 % higher than with Gray coding; program E5 measures exactly this.

InteractiveLabel the constellation

Lines join nearest neighbours: green = 1 bit differs, orange = 2, red = 3 or more. Switch to Gray and every line turns green.

Worked examplesSolved numericals

Example 1 · 3-bit Gray code construction
Given: reflect-and-prefix from 2 bits.

00, 01, 11, 10 → 000, 001, 011, 010, 110, 111, 101, 100.

Answer: the 8 codes listed.

Example 2 · Conversions XOR
Given: binary 1011 to Gray; Gray 1101 to binary.

\(1011\oplus0101=1110\). For 1101: \(b_3=1,\ b_2=1\oplus1=0,\ b_1=0\oplus0=0,\ b_0=0\oplus1=1\).

Answer: 1110 and 1001.

Example 3 · BER from SER Gray
Given: 16-QAM, SER \(=10^{-3}\).

\(P_b\approx10^{-3}/4\).

Answer: 2.5 × 10⁻⁴.

Example 4 · Natural 8-PSK penalty average Hamming distance
Given: labels 0…7 in order.

Neighbour differences 1,2,1,3,1,2,1,3; mean 1.75.

Answer: BER is 1.75× the Gray value (simulated: 1.75).

Example 5 · Natural 16-QAM penalty per axis
Given: 2-bit natural labels 00, 01, 10, 11 on each axis.

Neighbour pairs differ in 1, 2, 1 bits: mean 4/3.

Answer: ≈ 1.33× (simulated: 1.32).

Real worldWhere you meet this

Every standard

LTE, 5G NR, Wi-Fi and DVB all specify Gray-mapped QAM tables.

Rotary encoders

Position sensors use Gray codes so a reading caught mid-transition is off by one step, never by many.

Karnaugh maps

Rows and columns are Gray-ordered for exactly the same "one bit per step" reason.

Common mistakesWatch out

  • Gray-coding the 16-QAM labels as one 4-bit sequence along a snake path instead of I and Q separately.
  • Assuming BER = SER/k at low SNR, where errors to non-nearest neighbours are common.
  • Forgetting to Gray-decode at the receiver.

BER from SER\(P_b=\bar hP_s/k\)
Gray\(\bar h=1\Rightarrow P_b\approx P_s/k\)
Binary → Gray\(g=b\oplus(b\gg1)\)
Gray → binary\(b_i=b_{i+1}\oplus g_i\)
QAM labels\((g_I\ll k/2)\,|\,g_Q\)
Natural 8-PSK\(\bar h=1.75\)

Lecture 7 · M2 Digital Modulation · CO2

Which modulation does your phone use right now? It depends on the second

Phones and access points change modulation every few milliseconds: QPSK at the cell edge, 256-QAM near the tower, 1024-QAM when the channel is excellent. This lecture connects the theory to 5G NR, Wi-Fi 6/7, satellite and IoT radios.

Explain adaptive modulation and codingRead 5G NR and Wi-Fi modulation tablesCompute a Wi-Fi data rateChoose a modulation for a given channel and amplifier
⏱ 50 minBTL-4 Analyse

ConceptThe menu of modern systems

SystemModulationsWhy
5G NR (3GPP)π/2-BPSK, QPSK, 16-, 64-, 256-QAM; 1024-QAM downlink from Release 17Adaptive: robust at the edge, fast near the cell
LTEQPSK to 256-QAM (1024-QAM added later)Same idea, earlier generation
Wi-Fi 6 (802.11ax)BPSK to 1024-QAMShort, high-SNR indoor links
Wi-Fi 7 (802.11be)up to 4096-QAM20 % more bits per symbol than 1024-QAM
DVB-S2/S2X satelliteQPSK, 8-PSK, 16- to 256-APSKRings of points tolerate a non-linear satellite amplifier
GSM / Bluetooth LEGMSK / GFSKConstant envelope: cheap, efficient amplifiers
LoRa (IoT)Chirp spread spectrumWorks below the noise floor, very low rate

Adaptive modulation and coding (AMC)

The phone reports channel quality (CQI); the base station picks a modulation and code rate (MCS) for the next slot. Throughput tracks the channel instead of being fixed by the worst case.

The two limits

Noise sets how many points you can separate (this module). The power amplifier sets how much amplitude variation you can afford: hence constant-envelope schemes for battery and satellite links.

DerivationThroughput, MCS and the gap to Shannon

  1. Bits per resource element with modulation order \(M\) and code rate \(r\):

    \[ \eta_{\text{RE}}=r\log_2M\ \text{bit} \]

  2. OFDM data rate (Wi-Fi, 5G): \(N_{sd}\) data subcarriers, symbol duration \(T_{\text{sym}}\) including the guard interval, \(N_{ss}\) spatial streams:

    \[ R=\frac{N_{sd}\,\log_2M\;r\;N_{ss}}{T_{\text{sym}}} \]

  3. Example of the rule: 802.11ax, 80 MHz, 980 data subcarriers, 1024-QAM, \(r=5/6\), \(T_{\text{sym}}=12.8+0.8=13.6\ \mu\)s, one stream:

    \[ R=\frac{980\times10\times\tfrac56}{13.6\ \mu\text{s}}=600.5\ \text{Mb/s} \]

  4. Gap to Shannon. Uncoded QAM at BER \(10^{-5}\) needs about 7.5 dB more SNR than \(C=\log_2(1+\text{SNR})\) (program E7). Modern LDPC and polar codes (Module 5) recover most of this, leaving 1–2 dB.

  5. Diminishing returns. 256 → 1024-QAM adds 2 bits (25 %) but needs about 6 dB more SNR, and a transmitter EVM better than about 2 %. That is why 1024- and 4096-QAM only appear on short, clean links.

InteractiveLink adaptation: walk away from the tower

Model: 46 dBm transmitter, path loss 128.1 + 37.6 log₁₀(d km) dB (3GPP-style macro model), receiver noise figure 7 dB, no interference. MCS thresholds are illustrative values for teaching, not a 3GPP CQI table.

Worked examplesSolved numericals

Example 1 · Wi-Fi 6 rate OFDM rate formula
Given: 80 MHz, 980 data subcarriers, 1024-QAM, rate 5/6, 13.6 µs symbol, 1 stream.

\(980\times10\times5/6=8167\) bits per symbol; \(/13.6\ \mu\text{s}\).

Answer: 600.5 Mb/s (the MCS 11 rate).

Example 2 · 5G NR spectral efficiency MCS
Given: 256-QAM with code rate 948/1024.

\(8\times0.926=7.41\) bits per resource element.

Answer: 7.41 bit/RE (the top 256-QAM entry).

Example 3 · 1024-QAM gain diminishing returns
Given: 256-QAM → 1024-QAM at the same code rate.

Bits per symbol \(10/8=1.25\); required SNR rises by about \(10\log(1023/255)=6.0\) dB.

Answer: +25 % throughput for ≈ 6 dB more SNR.

Example 4 · EVM budget transmitter quality
Given: 4096-QAM needs EVM ≤ −38 dB.

\(10^{-38/20}=0.0126\).

Answer: 1.26 % rms.

Example 5 · Pick a modulation design
Given: Battery IoT sensor, 10 km, 1 kb/s.

Low SNR and low cost: a constant-envelope, robust scheme (GFSK, LoRa CSS, or π/2-BPSK in NB-IoT) rather than QAM.

Answer: constant-envelope, low-order modulation.

Lecture 8 · Lab · M2 Digital Modulation · CO2

Lab: simulate BPSK and QPSK over AWGN and beat the theory curve

The syllabus lab. Write about 30 lines of Python, send two million bits through a noisy channel, count the errors, and see your dots land on \(Q(\sqrt{2E_b/N_0})\).

Generate bits, map, add calibrated noiseCount errors and estimate BERPlot simulation against theoryExplain why BPSK and QPSK match
⏱ 2 h labBTL-3 Apply

ProcedureAim, equipment and plan

Aim

Simulate BPSK and QPSK over an AWGN channel, plot BER against Eb/N0 from 0 to 10 dB and verify against theory.

You need

Python 3.9+ with numpy, scipy, matplotlib (or MATLAB / GNU Octave). Any laptop; the full run takes under a minute.

  1. Bits: b = rng.integers(0, 2, N).

  2. Map: BPSK \(s=2b-1\) (so \(E_b=1\)); QPSK \(s=[(2b_1-1)+j(2b_2-1)]/\sqrt2\) (so \(E_s=1,\ E_b=\tfrac12\)).

  3. Noise: for a given \(E_b/N_0\), \(N_0=E_b/(E_b/N_0)\); real noise has \(\sigma^2=N_0/2\); complex noise has \(N_0/2\) on I and on Q.

  4. Detect: sign of the real part (and imaginary part for QPSK).

  5. Count: BER = errors / bits. Keep going until ≥ 100 errors at the highest \(E_b/N_0\).

  6. Compare: plot on a log scale with the theory curve \(Q(\sqrt{2E_b/N_0})=\tfrac12\text{erfc}(\sqrt{E_b/N_0})\).

ResultsWhat a correct run gives

Observation table (captured output)

At 10 dB only about 10 errors occur in 2 million bits, so that point scatters (±30 %). Use 10⁸ bits for a tight estimate there.

Python · e3_ber_bpsk_qpsk.py numpy, scipy, matplotlib
"""E3  Syllabus lab: BPSK and QPSK over AWGN, Monte-Carlo BER versus theory (Module 2, CO2).
Baseband (complex-envelope) simulation; one sample per symbol is exact for AWGN.
Requires: numpy, scipy, matplotlib.   Run: python e3_ber_bpsk_qpsk.py"""
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from scipy.special import erfc

Q = lambda x: 0.5*erfc(x/np.sqrt(2))
rng = np.random.default_rng(2026)
EbN0_dB = np.arange(0, 11)
nbits = 2_000_000

def bpsk(EbN0):
    b = rng.integers(0, 2, nbits)
    s = 2*b - 1                                     # Eb = 1
    n = rng.normal(0, np.sqrt(1/(2*EbN0)), nbits)    # sigma^2 = N0/2
    return np.mean(((s + n) > 0) != b)

def qpsk(EbN0):
    b = rng.integers(0, 2, nbits).reshape(-1, 2)
    s = ((2*b[:, 0]-1) + 1j*(2*b[:, 1]-1))/np.sqrt(2)  # Es = 1, Eb = 1/2 (Gray: one bit per axis)
    N0 = 0.5/EbN0
    n = np.sqrt(N0/2)*(rng.normal(size=s.size) + 1j*rng.normal(size=s.size))
    r = s + n
    bh = np.c_[r.real > 0, r.imag > 0]
    return np.mean(bh != b)

print(f"{'Eb/N0 dB':>8s} {'BPSK sim':>10s} {'QPSK sim':>10s} {'Q(sqrt(2Eb/N0))':>16s} {'errors (BPSK)':>14s}")
rows = []
for d in EbN0_dB:
    g = 10**(d/10)
    pb, pq, th = bpsk(g), qpsk(g), Q(np.sqrt(2*g))
    rows.append((d, pb, pq, th))
    print(f"{d:8d} {pb:10.3e} {pq:10.3e} {th:16.3e} {int(round(pb*nbits)):14d}")
rows = np.array(rows)
x = np.linspace(0, 11, 200)
plt.figure(figsize=(7.5, 5))
plt.semilogy(x, Q(np.sqrt(2*10**(x/10))), 'k-', label='theory  Q(√(2Eb/N0))')
plt.semilogy(rows[:, 0], rows[:, 1], 'o', mfc='none', ms=9, label='BPSK simulated')
plt.semilogy(rows[:, 0], rows[:, 2], 'x', ms=8, label='QPSK simulated')
plt.ylim(1e-7, 0.5); plt.grid(which='both', alpha=.35)
plt.xlabel('Eb/N0 (dB)'); plt.ylabel('BER'); plt.title('BPSK and QPSK have the same BER per bit')
plt.legend(); plt.tight_layout(); plt.savefig('../img/e3_ber.png', dpi=110)
need = x[np.argmax(Q(np.sqrt(2*10**(x/10))) < 1e-6)]
print(f"Eb/N0 needed for BER 1e-6: {need:.2f} dB")

% Runs in MATLAB or GNU Octave; needs no toolbox (Q-function written with erfc).
clear; clc; rng_seed = 2026; randn('seed', rng_seed); rand('seed', rng_seed);
Qf = @(x) 0.5*erfc(x/sqrt(2));
EbN0dB = 0:10; nbits = 1e6;
ber_b = zeros(size(EbN0dB)); ber_q = ber_b;
for i = 1:numel(EbN0dB)
    g = 10^(EbN0dB(i)/10);
    % BPSK, Eb = 1
    b = rand(1, nbits) > 0.5;  s = 2*b - 1;
    r = s + sqrt(1/(2*g))*randn(1, nbits);
    ber_b(i) = mean((r > 0) ~= b);
    % QPSK, Es = 1, Eb = 1/2, Gray: one bit on I, one on Q
    b2 = rand(2, nbits/2) > 0.5;
    s2 = ((2*b2(1,:) - 1) + 1j*(2*b2(2,:) - 1))/sqrt(2);
    N0 = 0.5/g;
    r2 = s2 + sqrt(N0/2)*(randn(1, nbits/2) + 1j*randn(1, nbits/2));
    ber_q(i) = mean([real(r2) > 0; imag(r2) > 0] ~= b2, 'all');
    fprintf('%3d dB  BPSK %.3e  QPSK %.3e  theory %.3e\n', EbN0dB(i), ber_b(i), ber_q(i), Qf(sqrt(2*g)));
end
x = linspace(0, 11, 200);

VivaViva questions

  1. Why do BPSK and QPSK give the same BER per bit?
  2. How is the noise standard deviation set from Eb/N0 for real and complex signals?
  3. Why does one sample per symbol suffice in this simulation?
  4. Your 10 dB point is far from theory. Why, and how do you fix it?
  5. What would change for 16-QAM?
  6. What is erfc and how is it related to Q(x)?

Common mistakesWatch out

  • Using σ² = N0 instead of N0/2.
  • Normalising QPSK to Es = 1 but forgetting that Eb = 1/2.
  • Computing BER from too few errors.

Python · e1_constellations.py numpy, matplotlib
"""E1  Gray-coded constellations: BPSK, QPSK, 8-PSK, 16-QAM, 64-QAM (Module 2, CO2).
Every constellation is normalised to unit average symbol energy Es = 1.
Requires: Python 3.9+, numpy, matplotlib.   Run: python e1_constellations.py"""
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

def gray(n):                      # n-bit Gray code of integer n
    return n ^ (n >> 1)

def psk(M):
    k = np.arange(M)
    pts = np.exp(1j*(2*np.pi*k/M + (np.pi/M if M == 4 else 0)))   # QPSK rotated by 45 degrees
    labels = np.zeros(M, int)
    labels[[gray(i) for i in range(M)]] = k                         # point index for each Gray label
    return pts, {int(gray(i)): pts[i] for i in range(M)}

def qam(M):
    m = int(np.sqrt(M)); b = int(np.log2(m))
    lev = np.arange(-(m-1), m, 2)                                    # -3,-1,1,3 for 16-QAM
    pts = {}
    for i in range(m):
        for q in range(m):
            label = (gray(i) << b) | gray(q)                         # Gray on I bits, Gray on Q bits
            pts[label] = lev[i] + 1j*lev[q]
    Es = np.mean(np.abs(list(pts.values()))**2)                      # = 2(M-1)/3
    return {k: v/np.sqrt(Es) for k, v in pts.items()}, Es

fig, ax = plt.subplots(1, 5, figsize=(17, 3.8))
print(f"{'scheme':>7s} {'bits/sym':>8s} {'Es(raw)':>8s} {'d_min (Es=1)':>13s} {'max Hamming between neighbours':>31s}")
for a, (name, M) in zip(ax, [('BPSK', 2), ('QPSK', 4), ('8-PSK', 8), ('16-QAM', 16), ('64-QAM', 64)]):
    k = int(np.log2(M))
    if 'QAM' in name:
        mp, Es = qam(M)
    else:
        _, mp = psk(M); Es = 1.0
    lab = np.array(list(mp.keys())); pt = np.array(list(mp.values()))
    D = np.abs(pt[:, None] - pt[None, :]); np.fill_diagonal(D, np.inf); dmin = D.min()
    near = np.isclose(D, dmin)                                       # nearest-neighbour pairs
    ham = max(bin(int(lab[i]) ^ int(lab[j])).count('1') for i, j in zip(*np.nonzero(near)))
    print(f"{name:>7s} {k:8d} {Es:8.2f} {dmin:13.4f} {ham:31d}")
    a.scatter(pt.real, pt.imag, s=30 if M < 64 else 12, color='C0')
    if M <= 16:
        for l, z in mp.items():
            a.annotate(format(l, f'0{k}b'), (z.real, z.imag), textcoords='offset points', xytext=(0, 7), ha='center', fontsize=9)
    a.axhline(0, color='0.6', lw=.6); a.axvline(0, color='0.6', lw=.6)
    a.set(title=f'{name}  ({k} bit/sym)', xlabel='I', ylabel='Q', aspect='equal', xlim=(-1.35, 1.35), ylim=(-1.35, 1.35)); a.grid(alpha=.3)
fig.tight_layout(); fig.savefig('../img/e1_constellations.png', dpi=110)

Python · e2_bpsk_waveform.py numpy, scipy
"""E2  BPSK: waveform, correlator receiver and power spectral density (Module 2, CO2).
Requires: numpy, scipy, matplotlib.   Run: python e2_bpsk_waveform.py"""
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from scipy.signal import welch

rng = np.random.default_rng(1)
Rb, fc, sps = 1e3, 4e3, 64              # bit rate, carrier, samples per bit
fs = Rb*sps; Tb = 1/Rb; Eb = 1.0
A = np.sqrt(2*Eb/Tb)                    # amplitude so that each bit carries energy Eb
bits = rng.integers(0, 2, 2000)
a = 2*bits - 1                          # 0 -> -1, 1 -> +1
t = np.arange(len(bits)*sps)/fs
s = A*np.repeat(a, sps)*np.cos(2*np.pi*fc*t)

EbN0 = 4.0                              # dB
N0 = Eb/10**(EbN0/10)
r = s + rng.normal(0, np.sqrt(N0/2*fs), s.size)   # white noise of PSD N0/2 at sample rate fs

phi = np.sqrt(2/Tb)*np.cos(2*np.pi*fc*t)          # unit-energy basis function
z = (r*phi).reshape(-1, sps).sum(1)/fs            # correlator output, one value per bit
bhat = (z > 0).astype(int)
print(f"Correlator output mean for '1': {z[bits==1].mean():+.3f}  (theory +sqrt(Eb) = +1.000)")
print(f"Correlator output std dev      : {z[bits==1].std():.3f}  (theory sqrt(N0/2) = {np.sqrt(N0/2):.3f})")
print(f"Bit errors: {np.sum(bhat!=bits)} of {bits.size}  -> BER = {np.mean(bhat!=bits):.4f}")

f, P = welch(s, fs, nperseg=4096)
fig, ax = plt.subplots(3, 1, figsize=(10, 8))
n = 8*sps
ax[0].plot(t[:n]*1e3, s[:n]); ax[0].step(np.arange(9)*Tb*1e3, np.r_[a[:8], a[7]]*A, 'r--', where='post')
ax[0].set(title='BPSK waveform (red: bit sequence)', xlabel='t (ms)')
ax[1].hist(z[bits==0], 60, alpha=.6, label="sent 0"); ax[1].hist(z[bits==1], 60, alpha=.6, label="sent 1")
ax[1].axvline(0, color='k'); ax[1].legend(); ax[1].set(title=f'Correlator output at Eb/N0 = {EbN0} dB', xlabel='z')
ax[2].semilogy(f/1e3, P/P.max()); ax[2].set(xlim=(0, 8), ylim=(1e-4, 2), title='PSD: sinc² main lobe fc ± Rb (null-to-null 2Rb)', xlabel='f (kHz)')
for x in ax: x.grid(alpha=.4)
fig.tight_layout(); fig.savefig('../img/e2_bpsk.png', dpi=110)

"""E3  Syllabus lab: BPSK and QPSK over AWGN, Monte-Carlo BER versus theory (Module 2, CO2).
Baseband (complex-envelope) simulation; one sample per symbol is exact for AWGN.
Requires: numpy, scipy, matplotlib.   Run: python e3_ber_bpsk_qpsk.py"""
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from scipy.special import erfc

Q = lambda x: 0.5*erfc(x/np.sqrt(2))
rng = np.random.default_rng(2026)
EbN0_dB = np.arange(0, 11)
nbits = 2_000_000

def bpsk(EbN0):
    b = rng.integers(0, 2, nbits)
    s = 2*b - 1                                     # Eb = 1
    n = rng.normal(0, np.sqrt(1/(2*EbN0)), nbits)    # sigma^2 = N0/2
    return np.mean(((s + n) > 0) != b)

def qpsk(EbN0):
    b = rng.integers(0, 2, nbits).reshape(-1, 2)
    s = ((2*b[:, 0]-1) + 1j*(2*b[:, 1]-1))/np.sqrt(2)  # Es = 1, Eb = 1/2 (Gray: one bit per axis)
    N0 = 0.5/EbN0
    n = np.sqrt(N0/2)*(rng.normal(size=s.size) + 1j*rng.normal(size=s.size))
    r = s + n
    bh = np.c_[r.real > 0, r.imag > 0]
    return np.mean(bh != b)

print(f"{'Eb/N0 dB':>8s} {'BPSK sim':>10s} {'QPSK sim':>10s} {'Q(sqrt(2Eb/N0))':>16s} {'errors (BPSK)':>14s}")
rows = []
for d in EbN0_dB:
    g = 10**(d/10)
    pb, pq, th = bpsk(g), qpsk(g), Q(np.sqrt(2*g))
    rows.append((d, pb, pq, th))
    print(f"{d:8d} {pb:10.3e} {pq:10.3e} {th:16.3e} {int(round(pb*nbits)):14d}")
rows = np.array(rows)
x = np.linspace(0, 11, 200)
plt.figure(figsize=(7.5, 5))
plt.semilogy(x, Q(np.sqrt(2*10**(x/10))), 'k-', label='theory  Q(√(2Eb/N0))')
plt.semilogy(rows[:, 0], rows[:, 1], 'o', mfc='none', ms=9, label='BPSK simulated')
plt.semilogy(rows[:, 0], rows[:, 2], 'x', ms=8, label='QPSK simulated')
plt.ylim(1e-7, 0.5); plt.grid(which='both', alpha=.35)
plt.xlabel('Eb/N0 (dB)'); plt.ylabel('BER'); plt.title('BPSK and QPSK have the same BER per bit')
plt.legend(); plt.tight_layout(); plt.savefig('../img/e3_ber.png', dpi=110)
need = x[np.argmax(Q(np.sqrt(2*10**(x/10))) < 1e-6)]

Python · e4_mpsk_mqam_ser.py numpy, scipy
"""E4  M-PSK and M-QAM: symbol and bit error rate, simulation versus the standard formulas (Module 2, CO2).
Requires: numpy, scipy, matplotlib.   Run: python e4_mpsk_mqam_ser.py"""
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from scipy.special import erfc

Q = lambda x: 0.5*erfc(x/np.sqrt(2))
rng = np.random.default_rng(7)
gray = lambda n: n ^ (n >> 1)

def const(kind, M):
    if kind == 'PSK':
        pts = np.exp(1j*(2*np.pi*np.arange(M)/M + np.pi/M))
        lab = np.array([gray(i) for i in range(M)])
    else:
        m = int(np.sqrt(M)); b = int(np.log2(m)); lev = np.arange(-(m-1), m, 2)
        I, Qv = np.meshgrid(np.arange(m), np.arange(m), indexing='ij')
        pts = (lev[I] + 1j*lev[Qv]).ravel()
        lab = ((np.vectorize(gray)(I) << b) | np.vectorize(gray)(Qv)).ravel()
    pts = pts/np.sqrt(np.mean(np.abs(pts)**2))
    return pts, lab

def theory(kind, M, EbN0):
    k = np.log2(M); Es = k*EbN0
    if kind == 'PSK':
        return 2*Q(np.sqrt(2*Es)*np.sin(np.pi/M)) if M > 2 else Q(np.sqrt(2*Es))
    p = 2*(1 - 1/np.sqrt(M))*Q(np.sqrt(3*Es/(M - 1)))
    return 1 - (1 - p)**2

def sim(kind, M, EbN0, nsym=400_000):
    pts, lab = const(kind, M); k = int(np.log2(M))
    idx = rng.integers(0, M, nsym)
    N0 = 1/(k*EbN0)
    r = pts[idx] + np.sqrt(N0/2)*(rng.normal(size=nsym) + 1j*rng.normal(size=nsym))
    det = np.argmin(np.abs(r[:, None] - pts[None, :]), axis=1)    # minimum-distance detector
    ser = np.mean(det != idx)
    xor = lab[det] ^ lab[idx]
    ber = np.mean([bin(v).count('1') for v in xor])/k
    return ser, ber

x = np.arange(0, 21, 2)
fig, ax = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(12, 4.8))
print(f"{'scheme':>7s} {'Eb/N0':>5s} {'SER sim':>9s} {'SER th':>9s} {'BER sim':>9s} {'SER/k':>9s}")
for kind, M in [('PSK', 4), ('PSK', 8), ('PSK', 16), ('QAM', 16), ('QAM', 64)]:
    name = f'{M}-{kind}'
    S, B = [], []
    for d in x:
        g = 10**(d/10); s, b = sim(kind, M, g); S.append(s); B.append(b)
        if d in (10, 14):
            print(f"{name:>7s} {d:5d} {s:9.2e} {theory(kind, M, g):9.2e} {b:9.2e} {theory(kind, M, g)/np.log2(M):9.2e}")
    xx = np.linspace(0, 20, 200)
    l, = ax[0].semilogy(xx, theory(kind, M, 10**(xx/10)), label=name)
    ax[0].semilogy(x, S, 'o', mfc='none', color=l.get_color())
    ax[1].semilogy(x, np.maximum(B, 1e-7), 'o-', mfc='none', color=l.get_color(), label=name)
for a, t in zip(ax, ['Symbol error rate (lines: formula, o: simulation)', 'Bit error rate with Gray mapping (simulated)']):
    a.set(ylim=(1e-6, 1), xlabel='Eb/N0 (dB)', title=t); a.grid(which='both', alpha=.35); a.legend()
fig.tight_layout(); fig.savefig('../img/e4_ser.png', dpi=110)

Python · e5_gray_vs_natural.py numpy
"""E5  Gray mapping versus natural binary mapping for 8-PSK and 16-QAM (Module 2, CO2).
Requires: numpy, matplotlib.   Run: python e5_gray_vs_natural.py"""
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

rng = np.random.default_rng(11)
gray = lambda n: n ^ (n >> 1)

def build(kind, M, use_gray):
    if kind == 'PSK':
        pts = np.exp(1j*2*np.pi*np.arange(M)/M)
        lab = np.array([gray(i) if use_gray else i for i in range(M)])
    else:
        m = int(np.sqrt(M)); b = int(np.log2(m)); lev = np.arange(-(m-1), m, 2)
        I, Qv = np.meshgrid(np.arange(m), np.arange(m), indexing='ij')
        f = np.vectorize(gray) if use_gray else (lambda v: v)
        pts = (lev[I] + 1j*lev[Qv]).ravel(); lab = ((f(I) << b) | f(Qv)).ravel()
    return pts/np.sqrt(np.mean(np.abs(pts)**2)), lab

def ber(kind, M, use_gray, EbN0_dB, n=300_000):
    pts, lab = build(kind, M, use_gray); k = int(np.log2(M)); N0 = 1/(k*10**(EbN0_dB/10))
    i = rng.integers(0, M, n)
    r = pts[i] + np.sqrt(N0/2)*(rng.normal(size=n) + 1j*rng.normal(size=n))
    d = np.argmin(np.abs(r[:, None] - pts[None, :]), 1)
    x = lab[d] ^ lab[i]
    bits = sum(((x >> j) & 1) for j in range(k))
    return np.mean(d != i), bits.mean()/k

x = np.arange(4, 19, 2)
plt.figure(figsize=(7.5, 5))
print(f"{'scheme':>8s} {'map':>8s} {'Eb/N0':>6s} {'SER':>9s} {'BER':>9s} {'BER/(SER/k)':>12s}")
for kind, M in [('PSK', 8), ('QAM', 16)]:
    for g in (True, False):
        B = []
        for d in x:
            s, b = ber(kind, M, g, d); B.append(b)
            if d == 12: print(f"{str(M)+'-'+kind:>8s} {'Gray' if g else 'natural':>8s} {d:6d} {s:9.2e} {b:9.2e} {b/(s/np.log2(M)):12.2f}")
        plt.semilogy(x, B, ('o-' if g else 's--'), mfc='none', label=f"{M}-{kind} {'Gray' if g else 'natural'}")
plt.grid(which='both', alpha=.35); plt.xlabel('Eb/N0 (dB)'); plt.ylabel('BER'); plt.legend()
plt.title('Same symbol errors, more bit errors without Gray coding'); plt.tight_layout(); plt.savefig('../img/e5_gray.png', dpi=110)

E616-QAM impairments and EVM

Output (captured from the run)

                          impairment   EVM %  EVM dB
                     AWGN, SNR 25 dB    5.67   -24.9

   IQ imbalance: 1 dB gain, 5° phase   11.04   -19.1

Each impairment leaves its own fingerprint. The uncorrected frequency offset smears the points into rings.

Python · e6_impairments_evm.py numpy
"""E6  16-QAM constellation impairments and EVM: noise, phase offset, IQ imbalance, carrier frequency offset.
Requires: numpy, matplotlib.   Run: python e6_impairments_evm.py"""
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

rng = np.random.default_rng(5)
lev = np.array([-3, -1, 1, 3]); ref = (lev[:, None] + 1j*lev[None, :]).ravel(); ref /= np.sqrt(10)
n = 4000; x = ref[rng.integers(0, 16, n)]

def awgn(s, snr_db):
    N0 = 10**(-snr_db/10)
    return s + np.sqrt(N0/2)*(rng.normal(size=s.size) + 1j*rng.normal(size=s.size))

def evm(r, s):
    return 100*np.sqrt(np.mean(np.abs(r - s)**2)/np.mean(np.abs(s)**2))

cases = {
    'AWGN, SNR 25 dB': awgn(x, 25),
    'phase offset 8°': awgn(x*np.exp(1j*np.deg2rad(8)), 30),
    'IQ imbalance: 1 dB gain, 5° phase': awgn((1.122*x.real) + 1j*(np.sin(np.deg2rad(5))*x.real + np.cos(np.deg2rad(5))*x.imag), 30),
    'CFO 0.0005·Rs (rotating)': awgn(x*np.exp(1j*2*np.pi*0.0005*np.arange(n)), 30),
}
fig, ax = plt.subplots(1, 4, figsize=(17, 4.4))
print(f"{'impairment':>36s} {'EVM %':>7s} {'EVM dB':>7s}")
for a, (k, r) in zip(ax, cases.items()):
    e = evm(r, x)
    print(f"{k:>36s} {e:7.2f} {20*np.log10(e/100):7.1f}")
    a.plot(r.real, r.imag, '.', ms=2, alpha=.5); a.plot(ref.real, ref.imag, 'r+', ms=10)
    a.set(title=f'{k}\nEVM = {e:.1f} %', aspect='equal', xlim=(-1.6, 1.6), ylim=(-1.6, 1.6)); a.grid(alpha=.3)
fig.tight_layout(); fig.savefig('../img/e6_evm.png', dpi=110)

E7Adaptive modulation and the Shannon limit

Output (captured from the run)

   scheme bit/sym  SNR needed (dB)  Shannon SNR for same rate (dB) gap (dB)
     BPSK       1             9.59                            0.00     9.59
     QPSK       2            12.60                            4.77     7.83
   16-QAM       4            19.46                           11.76     7.69
   64-QAM       6            25.57                           17.99     7.57
  256-QAM       8            31.53                           24.07     7.47
 1024-QAM      10            37.47                           30.10     7.37

Uncoded QAM sits about 7.5 dB from Shannon at BER 10⁻⁵.

Python · e7_adaptive_modulation.py numpy, scipy
"""E7  Spectral efficiency versus SNR: fixed modulations, adaptive modulation and the Shannon limit (Module 2, CO2).
Target BER 1e-5; uncoded M-QAM thresholds from the standard approximation.
Requires: numpy, scipy, matplotlib.   Run: python e7_adaptive_modulation.py"""
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from scipy.special import erfc
from scipy.optimize import brentq

Q = lambda x: 0.5*erfc(x/np.sqrt(2))
def ber_qam(M, snr):                 # snr = Es/N0 (linear); square M-QAM, Gray, nearest-neighbour approx.
    if M == 2: return Q(np.sqrt(2*snr))
    if M == 4: return Q(np.sqrt(snr))
    k = np.log2(M); return 4/k*(1 - 1/np.sqrt(M))*Q(np.sqrt(3*snr/(M - 1)))

target = 1e-5
print(f"{'scheme':>9s} {'bit/sym':>7s} {'SNR needed (dB)':>16s} {'Shannon SNR for same rate (dB)':>31s} {'gap (dB)':>8s}")
th = []
for M in [2, 4, 16, 64, 256, 1024]:
    s = brentq(lambda d: ber_qam(M, 10**(d/10)) - target, -5, 60)
    k = np.log2(M); sh = 10*np.log10(2**k - 1)
    th.append((M, k, s)); print(f"{('BPSK' if M==2 else 'QPSK' if M==4 else str(M)+'-QAM'):>9s} {k:7.0f} {s:16.2f} {sh:31.2f} {s-sh:8.2f}")
snr = np.linspace(-5, 45, 400)
eff = np.zeros_like(snr)
for M, k, s in th: eff[snr >= s] = k
plt.figure(figsize=(8, 5))
plt.plot(snr, np.log2(1 + 10**(snr/10)), 'k', label='Shannon  log₂(1+SNR)')
plt.step(snr, eff, where='post', label='adaptive uncoded QAM, BER 1e-5')
for M, k, s in th: plt.plot(s, k, 'o'); plt.annotate(f'{M}-QAM' if M > 2 else 'BPSK', (s, k), xytext=(4, -12), textcoords='offset points')
plt.xlabel('SNR = Es/N0 (dB)'); plt.ylabel('bit/s/Hz (Nyquist pulses)'); plt.grid(alpha=.35); plt.legend()
plt.title('About 7.5 dB gap to Shannon: coding (M5) closes most of it'); plt.tight_layout(); plt.savefig('../img/e7_adaptive.png', dpi=110)

Fifteen questions, twenty-four problems, four projects

Quick checkFifteen questions (25 minutes)

1. A 2400-baud modem using 16-QAM has a bit rate of U · Easy

k = 4 bits/symbol.

2. The BER of coherent BPSK is R · Easy

Antipodal signals, d = 2√Eb.

3. QPSK compared with BPSK at the same bit rate needs U · Easy

Two bits per symbol, independent I and Q.

4. For M-PSK, d_min equals R · Easy

Chord between adjacent points.

5. The average energy of square M-QAM with level spacing 2d is Ap · Medium

Two PAM axes, each (m²−1)d²/3.

6. Gray coding ensures that U · Easy

So BER ≈ SER/k.

7. An EVM of 10 % corresponds to an SNR of about Ap · Easy

−20 log 0.1 = 20 dB.

8. A rotated QAM constellation indicates An · Easy

Rigid rotation of all points.

9. Orthogonal coherent BFSK needs, relative to BPSK, Ap · Medium

d² = 2Eb instead of 4Eb.

10. DPSK avoids U · Easy

Differential detection.

11. Eb/N0 for Pr = −90 dBm, NF = 4 dB, Rb = 1 Mb/s is Ap · Medium

−90 + 174 − 4 − 60 = 20 dB.

12. Going from 64-QAM to 256-QAM needs roughly Ap · Medium

M−1 grows by ≈ 4.

13. Which uses constant-envelope modulation? U · Easy

GMSK suits saturated amplifiers.

14. A BER simulation should continue until about Ap · Easy

1/√100 = 10 % uncertainty.

15. Shannon capacity of 1 MHz at SNR 0 dB is Ap · Easy

log₂(1+1) = 1 bit/s/Hz.

DescriptiveA1–A8

A1. List four advantages of digital over analog communication and one disadvantage. Explain regeneration with a sketch.

Solution faculty
Regeneration, coding, multiplexing/integration, encryption/processing; disadvantage: more bandwidth / synchronisation. Sketch: analog repeater amplifies signal+noise; digital repeater decides and re-transmits clean pulses (L1).

A2. Draw the BPSK transmitter and the correlator receiver. Derive the probability of bit error.

Solution faculty
NRZ level encoder → product modulator with cos ωct; receiver: multiply by φ(t), integrate over Tb, sample, threshold at 0. Pb = Q(√(2Eb/N0)) as in L2.

A3. Explain QPSK generation with a block diagram and show that its BER equals that of BPSK.

Solution faculty
Serial-to-parallel → two NRZ streams → I × cos, Q × (−sin) → sum. With Gray mapping each axis is independent BPSK with Eb per bit (L3).

A4. Derive the minimum distance and the approximate symbol error rate of M-PSK.

Solution faculty
dmin = 2√Es sin(π/M); two nearest neighbours; Ps ≈ 2Q(√(2Es/N0) sin π/M) (L3).

A5. Show that the average energy of square M-QAM is 2(M−1)d²/3 and derive its SER.

Solution faculty
Per-axis mean square of odd levels (m²−1)d²/3, doubled; PPAM = 2(1−1/√M)Q(d/σ); Ps = 1 − (1 − PPAM)² (L4).

A6. What is Gray coding? Gray-label an 8-PSK and a 16-QAM constellation and explain why BER ≈ SER/log₂M.

Solution faculty
Adjacent codes differ in one bit; reflect-and-prefix construction; QAM: Gray I index and Q index separately (L6).

A7. Define EVM. Sketch the constellation effects of phase offset, I/Q imbalance and frequency offset.

Solution faculty
EVM = rms error vector / rms reference; rotation; rectangle/parallelogram; rotating ring (L4, E6).

A8. Explain adaptive modulation and coding in 5G NR, and why 1024-QAM is only used near the base station.

Solution faculty
CQI feedback → MCS selection per slot; 1024-QAM needs ≈ 6 dB more SNR than 256-QAM and EVM ≈ 2 %, which only short, clean links provide (L7).

NumericalN1–N12

N1. A 4-PSK system sends 12 Mb/s with roll-off 0.2. Find the symbol rate, bandwidth and spectral efficiency.

Solution faculty
Rs = 6 Mbaud; B = 7.2 MHz; η = 1.67 bit/s/Hz.

N2. BPSK at Eb/N0 = 9 dB. Find the BER.

Solution faculty
Eb/N0 = 7.94; Q(√15.9) = Q(3.99) = 3.4 × 10⁻⁵.

N3. Find Eb/N0 (dB) needed by BPSK for BER 10⁻⁴.

Solution faculty
Q(x) = 10⁻⁴ → x = 3.719; Eb/N0 = x²/2 = 6.92 → 8.4 dB.

N4. An 8-PSK system has Es/N0 = 18 dB. Estimate SER and BER.

Solution faculty
√(2 × 63.1) sin 22.5° = 4.30; SER ≈ 2Q(4.30) = 1.7 × 10⁻⁵; BER ≈ 5.7 × 10⁻⁶.

N5. 16-QAM uses levels ±1, ±3 on I and Q. Find the average and peak symbol energy and the peak-to-average power ratio.

Solution faculty
Average Es = 2(16−1)/3 = 10; corner points 3² + 3² = 18; PAPR = 1.8 = 2.55 dB.

N6. Compare dmin of 16-QAM and 16-PSK at equal average energy (dB).

Solution faculty
0.632 vs 0.390 → 4.2 dB in favour of QAM.

N7. Received power −95 dBm, NF 5 dB, Rb = 2 Mb/s, QPSK. Find Eb/N0 and BER.

Solution faculty
−95 + 174 − 5 − 63.0 = 11.0 dB (12.6); BER = Q(√25.2) = Q(5.02) = 2.6 × 10⁻⁷.

N8. A 1500-byte packet over a link with BER 2 × 10⁻⁶. Find the packet error rate.

Solution faculty
L = 12 000; PER = 1 − (1 − 2 × 10⁻⁶)¹²⁰⁰⁰ = 0.0237.

N9. Convert binary 1101 to Gray and Gray 0111 to binary.

Solution faculty
1101 ⊕ 0110 = 1011; Gray 0111 → binary 0101.

N10. A transmitter shows EVM = 4 %. Which of QPSK, 16-, 64-, 256-QAM meet the 5G limits?

Solution faculty
Limits 17.5, 12.5, 8, 3.5 % → QPSK, 16-QAM, 64-QAM pass; 256-QAM fails.

N11. Wi-Fi: 468 data subcarriers (40 MHz), 64-QAM rate 3/4, 13.6 µs symbol, 2 streams. Find the data rate.

Solution faculty
468 × 6 × 0.75 × 2 / 13.6 µs = 309.7 Mb/s.

N12. How many bits must you simulate to estimate BER 10⁻⁶ within ±10 %?

Solution faculty
≥ 100 errors → 10⁸ bits.

VerificationWhat was checked, and what was not

  • Programs E1–E7 were run in Python 3.13 (numpy 2.5, scipy 1.18); the outputs and plots on this page are from those runs. E3 was also run in GNU Octave.
  • Every worked example and practice answer was recomputed numerically; required Eb/N0 values in L5 are numerical solutions of the listed formulas.
  • Interactive widgets run Monte-Carlo simulations in the browser with fixed seeds; small differences from the formulas at very low error rates are statistical.
  • Standards figures (5G EVM limits, Wi-Fi MCS 11 rate, Wi-Fi 7 EVM) were checked against public summaries; confirm exact clause numbers in the current 3GPP / IEEE documents before examinations.
  • The link-adaptation thresholds in L7 are illustrative teaching values, not the 3GPP CQI table.
